docs.title: SkinSense
docs.text:
Author(s):

Himantveer Kaur, Muskan Kohli, Ansh Bindal, Arnav Chandla

SkinSense is an AI-based skin analysis and skincare recommendation app. It predicts skin type and acne severity from a user-submitted photo, then generates a personalised skincare routine and product recommendations -- filtered by budget, allergies, and ingredient conflicts -- with weekly longitudinal tracking and a dermatologist-referral safety net for severe or low-confidence cases.

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text:
• code/backend -- FastAPI backend
  • code/frontend -- React (Vite) frontend
  • ml -- model training/inference code (skin type, acne severity)

docs.title: Criteria for Project Selection
docs.text: This document defines the criteria we will use to choose projects for our software engineering course. It emphasizes time-to-value through rapid iterations, supported by CI/CD to enable frequent build, test, and delivery. Selection also considers contextual relevance, available engineering engines, scalability, and measurable evaluation criteria to ensure we build solutions that can be validated quickly and effectively.

docs.title: Time-to-value
docs.text:
We shall design for rapid delivery, i.e. deliver meaningful increments within a short time window (say weekly). And, prioritize fast feedback over perfection, in order to reduce waiting time between decisions and results.

Initially, you may think of it as:

  • Ship a usable increment within 2 weeks.
  • Complete discovery + prototype + validation in one 2-week sprint.
  • Success is defined by what can be delivered in the first 2-week iteration.

docs.title: CI/ CD
docs.text:
You might have guessed that the core requirement of this project is to showcase multiple iterations of build, test, and ship, fast enough for user/ client to get quick feedback about the product.

To support our short weekly iteration cadence, we should automate build/test/release as much as practical. CI/CD is a good way to achieve that—starting with the lightest pipeline we can (e.g., CI first) and expanding only if it improves delivery.

docs.title: 1. Relevance
docs.text:
Contextual relevance: The problem affects our immediate stakeholders and is within our current scope to influence.

A rough equivalent of need statement. We shall prefer that your problem be of,

  • Local relevance, i.e, relevance to your local environment/region/team.
  • Immediate applicability, i.e, we can act on it now.
  • (to some extent) Near-term impact, i.e, its outcomes are soon visible.

docs.title: 2. Engine availability
docs.text:
This is an engineering course and not a research course. Hence, a necessary heuristic for selection, should be that one or more mature engine(s) should be available as an engine for the core solution of the problem.

We shall address the issues of scalability and complexity here, rather than fundamental algorithms itself. Intuitively, we’ll focus on administrative aspects of software development, more than operational or creative aspects.

PS: Research delays shall not be entertained.

docs.title: 3. Scalability
docs.text:
With foresight, your project should be scalable in the following contexts:

  1. Scalable: Theoretically speaking, your proposition should in principle scale to a larger audience than intended.
  2. Operationally Deployable: Practically speaking, your proposition should be deployable using the available solutions for an extremely large audience.

docs.title: 4. Evaluation Criterion
docs.text:
Evaluation criterion: How will we know it worked?

A good proposition/solution usually includes a way to judge whether the solution actually works.

The evaluation criterion should be measurable (and ideally attributable).

Examples

  • Problem: “Students can’t find answers fast.” Solution: “Add an FAQ search.” Evaluation criterion: “Search results find the correct answer within 10 seconds, and users report satisfaction ≥ 4/5.”

  • Problem: “The app is slow.” Solution: “Optimize queries.” Evaluation criterion: “Page load time decreases from 3s to under 1.5s in production.”

docs.title: 5. Higher-order goal
docs.text:
Treat this as a secondary heuristic, i.e. something to be fulfilled with a lower priority.

It can be very useful—but mostly as a framing layer, not as the whole engineering plan. A higher-order goal, /e.g./ address climate change, helps

  1. Guides priorities,
  2. Creates measurable outcomes,
  3. Makes the problem-solution link easier to justify.

But we still need to translate that why (climate change) into a measurable problem, e.g.

  • Reduce e-waste and “time-to-replace”
  • Reduce network energy and hardware load
  • Lower lifecycle impact by improving reliability (or durability)
  • Sustainable operations
  • Digital efficiency

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: In selecting a project, we prioritize measurable time-to-value through rapid, incremental delivery and fast feedback. CI/CD is the practical mechanism that makes shipping dependable. We focus on problems with contextual relevance, available engineering engines, and scalable, deployable solutions—validated through clear evaluation criteria—while keeping higher-order goals as supportive framing rather than primary drivers.

docs.title: Week 12 : Photo Validation and Merge to Master
Saving Predictions
docs.text: I connected the AnalysisResult table to /api/predict. Every prediction, whether it comes from a photo or from manual input, is now saved with the user, image id, skin type and confidence, acne severity and confidence, lesion estimate, source (model, stub or manual) and the referral flag.

docs.title: Test Fixes and Merge to Master
docs.text: Two predict tests started failing after the real inference work. /api/predict with an image_id now needs a skin_type, so the old tests got a 422 instead of the response they expected, and one of them also checked for source == "stub". The app was behaving correctly and the tests were outdated, so I updated them to send skin_type and to accept either stub or model as the source. I also added a test that a photo request without skin_type is rejected. After that everything passed, and I merged the integration branch (real inference, PostgreSQL and Alembic, the product catalog and the new frontend) into master with a pull request.

docs.title: MediaPipe Photo Validation
docs.text:
I replaced the validation stub, which returned ok: true for every file, with a real validate_photo that uses MediaPipe FaceMesh. The return format is the same as before (ok, reasons, checks, validator_version). A photo is rejected, with a message the user can act on, when:

  • the file cannot be read as an image
  • no face is found, or more than one face is found
  • the face is cut off at the edge of the photo or is too small in the frame
  • the head is turned too far to the side (I estimate yaw from where the nose sits between the two cheek landmarks)
  • the face region is too dark or too bright
  • the face is blurry (variance of the Laplacian on a face crop resized to 256 px)

Phone photos are rotated according to their EXIF data before the checks, because MediaPipe expects an upright face. The upload page already shows the reasons returned by the backend, so the frontend did not need any change.

The newest MediaPipe releases no longer include the mp.solutions API, which has the face models bundled inside the package. The replacement API needs a separate model file to be downloaded. I pinned mediapipe==0.10.21, the last version that has the bundled models. It needs numpy<2, so I pinned numpy==1.26.4 too and checked that the project's PyTorch version still works with it.

If MediaPipe cannot be imported, the validator lets photos through and reports mediapipe-unavailable as its version, so a broken install does not block the whole upload flow.

For testing, the face detector is a separate function, so the unit tests replace it with fake landmarks and cover each rejection reason without a real face photo. One more test runs the real MediaPipe on a blank image and checks that it finds no face. The existing upload test now stubs the validator, since a plain test image correctly fails validation. I also added a small command line helper (py -m services.photo_validation <image>) to check the thresholds on real photos.

docs.title: CI
docs.text: I added a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the backend tests and builds the frontend on every pull request and every push to master. The tests run in stub mode so the workflow does not need PyTorch.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The validation thresholds are starting values and need tuning on more real photos. The skin-type model is the next big ML task.

docs.title: Use-Case Modelling
docs.text:
I worked on the SkinSense use-case diagram. The main actors were defined as User and Admin.

For the User, I mapped the analysis flow from Upload Selfie for Analysis to Verify Face Photo, Predict Skin Type, Predict Acne Severity, and View Analysis Results. The recommendation-related functions were separated into Get Product Recommendations, Check Ingredient Conflicts, View Recommendation Explanation, Set Price Preference, Build AM/PM Routine, and View Safety Disclaimer.

For the Admin, I added Manage Product & Ingredient Database to represent maintenance of the product and ingredient information used by the recommendation engine.

Track Skin Progress was kept as a planned future feature because periodic tracking is not part of the current core implementation.

docs.title: Technical Review
docs.text: I checked the relationships between the use cases so that prediction functions support the analysis result and recommendation functions operate after analysis. PostgreSQL was not added as an actor because it is an internal database component.

docs.title: Reference Study
docs.text:
I reviewed the ACNE04 method used for the planned acne-severity model. The referenced preprocessing uses three severity classes: mild (1-5), moderate (6-20), and severe (>20). The method also applies class balancing, resizing, and normalization before model training.

No application code was written during this task.

docs.title: Backend Schemas and Storage
docs.text: I set up the request/response schemas for the upload and predict endpoints, along with the local storage handling for uploaded images. This gave the rest of the backend a fixed shape to build against before any real model logic existed.

docs.title: /api/upload and /api/predict
docs.text: I implemented /api/upload and /api/predict with stub inference wired in, plus the referral-flag logic (returning a placeholder "see a dermatologist" flag for now). The stub returns a deterministic response so the frontend team could build against a stable contract while the real ResNet-50 model was still in training.

docs.title: Integrating Ansh's Recommendation Router
docs.text: Once Ansh's stub recommendation engine and router were ready, I wired his router into main.py so the full request chain (upload → predict → recommend) worked end to end through one FastAPI app.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
I ran the backend and frontend together locally and walked through the full flow: uploading a photo, getting a stub severity/skin-type prediction, and receiving a stub product list with an AM/PM routine. This became the definition-of-done check for the week: a clean clone had to run both servers and complete the flow, including the manual-fallback path if a model step failed.

No trained models were involved yet; this week was purely about getting the skeleton running.

docs.title: Week 6 : Data Pipelines and First Training Run
ACNE04 Preprocessing
docs.text:
I preprocessed the ACNE04 dataset following the approach in the reference paper (Zhang and Ma). The steps were:

  • Relabelled the lesion counts into three severity classes: mild (1-5), moderate (6-20) and severe (>20).
  • Built the train/test split from the paper's fold 0 instead of a random split, so our numbers stay comparable to the paper.
  • Resized all images to 224x224 and normalized them with the ImageNet mean and std, since ResNet-50 starts from ImageNet weights.
  • Applied class-count smoothing, because the severe class has far fewer images than mild and moderate.
  • Checked the raw annotation format against the paper's description before running the relabelling script.
  • Checked that images from the same patient or session do not end up on both sides of the split. The 99%+ accuracy in the paper is most likely inflated by this kind of leakage, and we would rather report a lower number that holds up.

docs.title: Skin-Type Data Preparation
docs.text: With Muskan, I worked on the data side of the skin-type notebook. We finished collecting the dry class (about 250 images, with a source log) and cleaned the oily and normal classes taken from Kaggle by removing duplicates and fixing labels.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The ACNE04 split and the smoothing weights are what the first ResNet-50 run trains on. If the run's numbers look wrong, those are the first two things to check.

docs.title: PostgreSQL and Migrations
docs.text: Until this week the app was only really running on SQLite, even though Postgres was the plan. I set up PostgreSQL locally and added Alembic for migrations, so schema changes can be applied without editing the database by hand.

docs.title: AnalysisResult Model
docs.text: I added an AnalysisResult model and table to store each user's predictions (severity, skin type, confidence and timestamp). It is not connected to /api/predict yet, so for now the endpoint returns a prediction without saving it.

docs.title: Auth
docs.text: /api/predict and /api/recommendations are now behind JWT auth, and /api/ingredients stays public. Refresh tokens use token versioning so they can be revoked on logout. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt. I pinned bcrypt==4.0.1 because passlib==1.7.4 breaks on newer bcrypt versions.

docs.title: Real Acne Inference
docs.text:
I replaced the stub with the trained ResNet-50 checkpoint (resnet50_acne.pt). Loading it with the standard torchvision constructor failed with mismatched keys, because the checkpoint was saved from a feature-wrapped version of the model. I changed the loader to detect which format the checkpoint uses and build the matching model. The API now returns source: "model" for real predictions. The stub can still be used with the SKINSENSE_USE_REAL_MODELS flag.

There is no skin-type model yet, so /api/predict with a photo now needs a skin_type in the request. The backend uses that value with a confidence of 1.0.

docs.title: Product Catalog
docs.text: I built the product catalog from kingabzpro/cosmetics-datasets. The raw file had 1,472 rows and 1,325 were left after removing junk entries from the scrape. The ingredient reference list now has 25 ingredients, our original 12 plus 13 taken from the amaboh dataset. The seeded catalog has 1,333 products: the 1,325 real ones and 8 hand-written toner and serum entries, so those routine steps always have something to show.

docs.title: Merging Branches
docs.text: I merged Muskan's frontend branch into mine. The only conflict was in inference.py, where her branch still had the old stub version. I kept the real inference version.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: I ran the backend tests after each change (15 auth tests, 8 analysis tests, 10 recommendation tests and the health check), and all of them pass.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: AnalysisResult still needs to be connected to /api/predict. Photo validation is still the stub and the skin-type model is not trained yet.

docs.title: Gantt Chart
docs.text:
I worked on the SkinSense project timeline and checked the ordering of tasks according to technical dependencies.

The main sequence was arranged as:

Data Preparation -> Face Verification -> Model Training -> API Integration -> Recommendation Engine -> AM/PM Routine -> Testing -> Pilot Testing -> Refinement

Database schema design and product/ingredient data preparation were placed before the recommendation engine because the rule-based recommendation module depends on this data.

The timeline also separates the periodic skin-tracking feature from the core flow by marking it as a future/stretch feature.

I reviewed the supplied ACNE04 classification method. The approach uses ResNet-50 with skip connections and modified bottleneck blocks. The reviewed preprocessing includes severity reclassification, class balancing, image resizing, and normalization.

No application code was written during this task.

This meant the frontend was demoable even if a backend piece wasn't finished in time.

docs.title: Week 6 : Data Pipelines and First Training Run
ResNet-50 Training Script and First Run
docs.text:
I worked on the training side of the acne notebook with Himmat, using her preprocessed ACNE04 split and class smoothing. I wrote the training loop on an ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-50 with the last layer replaced by a 3-class severity head. For the loss I used weighted cross-entropy on top of the inverse-frequency smoothing, so the severe class, which is the smallest, still gets a useful gradient.

I ran it on Kaggle with GPU T4 x2 and Internet turned on, and used Save Version and Save & Run All so the run is committed and not lost if the laptop goes to sleep. The first run finished. I looked at the per-class confusion matrix and not only the overall accuracy, because with this much class imbalance a model that mostly predicts mild could still look fine on accuracy alone. This run is our baseline for the augmentation and loss experiments.

docs.title: Skin-Type Dataset
docs.text: I collected and cleaned the images for the skin-type classifier (oily, dry and normal). I removed duplicates and kept a source log for the images I collected manually.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: I saved the run logs and the per-class breakdown, so they can be used for error analysis later.

docs.title: Frontend Pages
docs.text:
I finished the remaining pages (Profile, Ingredients, About and Feedback), which made seven pages in total alongside Upload, Results and Recommendations, all in the shadcn/Mainline theme.

Later in the week I reworked the frontend into a shorter flow. Upload and Results were merged into one Analyze page, where the user can upload a photo or take one with the camera, pick a skin type, and add ingredients to avoid as tags. Recommendations became a Report page that shows the results with confidence, the filters, and a "Why this?" explanation on each product. I added a separate Routine page for the AM/PM routine, and removed the standalone Upload, Results, About and Ingredients pages. I also redid the base, theme and component styles to match.

docs.title: API Client
docs.text: I added silent token refresh to the API client, so an expired access token is refreshed in the background with the refresh token and the user is not sent back to login. The client now sends skin_type along with the photo request, since the backend needs it while there is no skin-type model. The fixture fallback still works on every page, so the app can be demoed even if the backend is down.

docs.title: Skin-Type Dataset
docs.text: I kept working on the skin-type dataset for the MobileNetV2 classifier. This week was about finalizing it: checking the image count per class, removing a few more duplicates that were missed in the first cleanup, and making sure the folder structure matches what the training notebook expects.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The dataset is ready. The MobileNetV2 training and combining it with the questionnaire scoring are still to do.
